title: Why AI Agents Need Persistent Browser Identities
content:
Randomizing browser fingerprints is easy. Keeping them consistent is hard.
AI agents rarely perform only one browser task. They authenticate, pause, return after a process restart, and sometimes run several unrelated workflows in parallel. Cookies and local storage matter, but they are only part of the browser identity that a site observes.
A browser also exposes related signals such as User-Agent, User-Agent Client Hints, platform, screen characteristics, hardware buckets, locale, time zone, graphics data, and network context. Changing one value independently can create contradictions. Changing values again on every launch can make the same agent look like a different browser after a reload.
The useful engineering question is therefore not just:
Can a browser report a different fingerprint?
It is:
Can one saved browser identity remain coherent and reproducible across time?
These ideas are easy to conflate:
- Masking changes selected browser-visible values.
- Consistency keeps related values coherent with one another.
- Persistence keeps the same profile identity and user state across later launches.
- Isolation prevents one profile from inheriting another profile's state.
Masking without consistency can produce a plausible-looking collection of contradictory values. Consistency without persistence still gives an agent a disposable session. Persistence without isolation risks mixing unrelated workflows.
Browser3 is a multi-profile antidetect Chromium browser for people and AI agents. Its primary differentiator is persistent, internally consistent browser identities. Native Chromium-level fingerprint masking is the implementation hook; consistency and persistence are what make each saved identity testable over time.
Each Browser3 profile combines a generated identity configuration with its own Chromium
user-data directory. The configuration has a persistent profile_id. Profile-specific
choices derive deterministically from that seed instead of fresh per-session randomness.
The user-data directory stores normal state such as cookies and web storage.
Selecting the same profile again reuses both:
.\browser3 --profile 1
Different profiles use separate user-data directories and profile locks. The intended mapping is simple:
one agent -> one persistent Browser3 profile
That mapping does not give an agent new permissions, solve authentication, or guarantee how a website will react. It creates a stable browser boundary that can be reproduced and debugged.
The Python layer probes the host, generates deterministic configuration, manages profiles, and launches the browser. It does not inject fingerprint JavaScript into pages. Browser-visible masking is implemented in the packaged native Chromium layer.
The public source boundary is deliberate: the repository exposes the MPL-2.0 orchestration, profile-generation policy, documentation, and release verification path. It does not expose the private native masking implementation or enough source to rebuild the distributed executable.
This distinction matters because a page-level JavaScript hook can change one readout without making related browser surfaces agree. Browser3 passes validated profile data to native browser code and preserves native behavior when a safe override is not available.
Normal launches are headful and CDP-free. Automation is opt-in through a loopback-only
CDP control path or the local Session API. In a five-profile Release measurement, an
active Playwright or Puppeteer client was visible to detector tooling as Developer
Tools in 5/5 profiles. That limitation is documented rather than treated as a
fingerprint-masking result.
The distributed Browser3 runtime is based on Chromium 149.0.7827.201. That does not
mean every browser surface reports the same four-part string.
The reduced User-Agent currently follows Chromium's reduced format and reports
149.0.0.0. High-entropy UA-CH and generated profile full-version values use
deterministic verified patches from 149.0.7827.196 through 149.0.7827.201.
Browser3 therefore does not claim exact .201 on every surface.
Hardware-bound capabilities, limits, color depth, and the ANGLE backend remain native. A GPU identity override is accepted only as one validated WebGL/WebGPU block; invalid data falls back to host behavior. Canvas and audio noise remain off by default because earlier testing detected them. The currently measured clean seeded diversity axes are text edging and font hiding.
The public lifecycle report is a dated observation for Browser3/Chromium
149.0.7827.201 on one physical Windows host and one network context. It used five
persistent profiles in a headful, CDP-free run without a proxy. It did not select one
favorable profile.
The 15/15 reload total represents five profiles across three process cycles. Raw
identifiers and raw profile signatures are not published.
The immutable r3 release then passed its own headful, CDP-free, no-proxy gate on
2026-08-20. All five profiles returned scores and reload measurements. The recorded
five-profile averages were 0.0412 for the Fingerprint.com tampering model, 0.0654
for its virtual-machine model, and 0.1250 for the optional VPN model. These numbers
are observations of those models on that release and host, not targets or bypass
guarantees.
The deeper public cross-check dated 2026-08-15 also kept adverse results visible:
These services measure different things and can change independently of Browser3. A visitor identifier, a tampering signal, a bot verdict, and a lifecycle comparison are not interchangeable metrics. The complete method and limitations are in the public validation report.
Use the official Windows x64 r3 release and verify the detached OpenPGP signature and
SHA-256 manifest. Browser3-owned PE files are not Authenticode-signed. Keep the complete
runtime\ directory intact and use a physical hardware-accelerated GPU.
For a gate-compatible direct-network run, launch all five profiles without a proxy:
.\browser3 --profile 1 --no-proxy
.\browser3 --profile 2 --no-proxy
.\browser3 --profile 3 --no-proxy
.\browser3 --profile 4 --no-proxy
.\browser3 --profile 5 --no-proxy
For each profile:
- Load the same test with a fresh document between observations.
- Compare only selected stable signals.
- Close and reopen the same profile.
- Start a new browser process and repeat.
- Compare the result with the other four profiles.
- Record the release, date, host context, proxy mode, and whether CDP was active.
Do not publish cookies, IP or geolocation data, proxy credentials, visitor/request IDs, personal data, or raw profile signatures. The internal harness and raw baselines remain private; the public report exposes sanitized aggregates and enough protocol detail to challenge the conclusion without exposing sensitive test data.
This is not a universal detector-evasion claim.
- The cited evidence covers one physical Windows host and one network context.
- The release gate ran without a proxy; proxy and multi-geo behavior were not part of that tested GO.
- Profiles are generated for the current machine and should not be moved to different hardware.
- The current runtime requires Windows x64 and a physical hardware-accelerated GPU.
- Widevine is not included; Windows N/KN may require the Media Feature Pack.
- The public source layer cannot rebuild the proprietary native executable.
- External detector models change over time, and the recorded results include mixed and unavailable outcomes.
Browser3 does not claim to be "undetectable" and does not guarantee an anti-bot bypass or a particular detector score.
Download the immutable
Browser3 v149.0.7827.201-r3 release
and follow the repository Quick Start. A Python 3.10+ client is
also published as browser3==0.1.0; the optional npm package
@radek-b3/browser3@0.1.0 is a thin wrapper around that Python client, not a separate
runtime.

report.summary: AI agents need persistent, coherent browser identities; Browser3 offers a multi-profile antidetect Chromium browser with deterministic, reproducible fingerprint profiles for reliable automation.
report.background: AI agents rarely perform a single browser task. They authenticate, pause, restart, and run multiple workflows in parallel. Cookies and local storage are only part of what a website observes; browsers also expose User-Agent, client hints, hardware characteristics, locale, time zone, and network context. Randomizing these values per session creates contradictions that make the same agent look like a different browser after each reload. The article distinguishes masking from consistency, persistence, and isolation. Most tools only mask, producing plausible but internally inconsistent identities. Browser3 addresses this by combining a deterministic profile seed with a dedicated Chromium user-data directory, making each identity stable and testable over time. The project is MPL-2.0 at the orchestration layer while keeping native fingerprint masking proprietary, a deliberate boundary for both usability and commercial protection.
key_points: Browser identity is not just cookies. Persistent AI agents need coherent combinations of User-Agent, client hints, screen properties, locales, and other signals that remain consistent across process restarts and parallel sessions. Randomizing each value independently creates contradictions that are easy to detect.

Masking, consistency, persistence, and isolation are separate engineering concerns. Masking changes values, consistency keeps related values coherent, persistence preserves identity across launches, and isolation prevents profiles from mixing state. A robust antidetect browser must address all four, not just masking.

Browser3 generates profile-specific choices deterministically from a persistent profile_id seed, paired with a native Chromium user-data directory. Reusing the same profile via `--profile 1` restores both configuration and state, enabling reproducible, debuggable sessions for one agent per profile.

The implementation avoids JavaScript injection. Fingerprint masking is implemented in the native Chromium layer, while the Python orchestration probes the host and launches the browser. This reduces the risk of page-level hooks that change one readout without aligning related browser surfaces.

Public validation is deliberately honest about limitations. The release gate measured five profiles on one Windows host without proxies, showing low tampering scores but not universal undetectability. The project documents CDP exposure and external detector variability rather than promising bypass guarantees.
report.impact: For AI developers, Browser3 offers a way to give agents stable browser identities that survive restarts and parallel workflows, potentially reducing bot detection and session failures. This is especially valuable for automation that requires long-lived logged-in sessions or multi-account operating without cross-contamination. However, the project explicitly does not guarantee anti-bot bypass, and its Windows-only, hardware-GPU requirement limits deployment scenarios. For regular users, persistent identity tools raise privacy and anti-fingerprinting possibilities, but the proprietary native layer means trust must be placed in the vendor. The broader industry takeaway is that persistent coherence matters more than one-off masking; expect antidetect tools to shift toward reproducible identity lifecycle management rather than simple spoofing.
report.tools: Follow the Browser3 repository for the MPL-2.0 orchestration logic and validation reports. The official Windows x64 r3 release is the current testable artifact. Python client `browser3==0.1.0` and npm wrapper `@radek-b3/browser3@0.1.0` are available. For comparison, watch Playwright and Puppeteer CDP-based automation patterns; Browser3's opt-in loopback CDP shows how standard tools can combine with persistent profiles.
